title: Task Lighting Upgrade in a Small Kitchen: Recessed Downlights and Under-Cabinet Fluorescents
summary: This Old House demonstrates a kitchen lighting retrofit aimed at improving task illumination in a small space. The hosts replace two dim, nearby ceiling fixtures with two recessed LED/fluorescent-ready downlights (referred to as R40 blimps) to bring light down to the counter, and add complementary under-cabinet and above-cabinet fluorescent lighting (Thin Line) to brighten work surfaces and shelves. The project covers planning around existing sprinklers and ceiling obstructions, routing power from a single switch, creating ceiling penetrations, mounting fixtures with clips, hiding cords through cabinet fronts and crown molding, and testing the system for a brighter, more usable kitchen workspace.

sections.description: The hosts observe a dim kitchen with two ceiling fixtures controlled by separate switches and acknowledge the inability to clearly see while chopping at the counter. They propose removing the existing fluorescents, installing two recessed downlights (R40 blimps) on a single switch, and adding above- and below-cabinet fluorescent lighting to improve task visibility.

sections.description: After turning off power, the team begins removing the existing fixtures and the ceiling bar that supports a junction box. They note a sprinkler pipe with a drop ceiling that limits clearance and take steps to create open space for the new recessed cans.

sections.description: Templates are used to mark and cut holes for two recessed lights. Remodel recessed fixtures are installed, secured with pressure clips, and wired in series so both cans operate from a single switch. Wires are routed between the two fixtures before the cans are pressed fully into the ceiling.

sections.description: With power restored and a plan to control both cabinet lights from the existing switch, the team routes wiring from the wall through the stud area and up to the tops of the cabinets. They introduce Thin Line fluorescent fixtures for both under- and over-cabinet lighting, align them back-to-front to minimize bulb visibility, and use mounting clips and an interconnect cable. When a rib in the cabinet interferes with the cord, they cut a small notch in the front edge to hide the wiring and create a clean knee joint for the cord.

sections.description: The power is reactivated and both the recessed ceiling lights and the cabinet lighting are tested. The hosts confirm a significant improvement in the kitchen’s task lighting and congratulate each other on the completed upgrade.
